1181.quote_or_event: “By the actions we have committed, we are separated from You. Please show Your Mercy, and unite us with Yourself, Lord.”
1181.explanation: In his Barah Maha (the song of the twelve months), Guru Arjan has the separated soul-bride admit that her separation comes from her own deeds, so she can only ask the Lord for mercy and reunion.
1181.tie_back: The Kural's wife admits she herself agreed to her husband's going and so has no one to complain to; the soul-bride in Gurbani likewise owns that the separation is her own doing and turns only to the Beloved.
1181.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 133, Raag Maajh, Barah Maha, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1181._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on a separation the speaker brought on herself, but the love is the soul's spiritual longing for God, not a wife's for a husband, and 'actions' means karma, not consent to a journey.

1182.quote_or_event: “Your actions seem so sweet to me.”
1182.explanation: Guru Arjan says that whatever the Lord does, including what brings pain, tastes sweet to the devotee, because it comes from Him.
1182.tie_back: The Kural's pallor spreads proudly over her body because it was given by her husband; Gurbani likewise finds even hardship sweet because the Beloved sent it.
1182.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1182._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable-to-strong fit on valuing an affliction because of who gave it, but the line is about accepting God's will (hukam), not the playful pride of a lover's pallor.

1183.quote_or_event: “So many endure distress, deprivation and constant abuse. Even these are Your Gifts, O Great Giver!”
1183.explanation: In Japji Sahib Guru Nanak counts even suffering and want among the gifts of the Giver, since they too come from His hand and can teach the soul.
1183.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her husband took her beauty and modesty and gave her love-sickness and pallor in exchange; Guru Nanak likewise calls pain and loss gifts of the Beloved Giver.
1183.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (pauri 25), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1183._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), two consecutive lines of pauri 25; reasonable fit on pain received as a gift, though the Kural's ironic 'exchange' between lovers has no counterpart in Japji's teaching on accepting God's will.

1184.quote_or_event: “I sing His Glories, I describe His Glories, I speak of His Glories, O my mother.”
1184.explanation: Guru Ram Das gives the voice of a soul-bride who fills her speech with the virtues of her Beloved, talking of nothing else.
1184.tie_back: The Kural's wife protests that she thinks only of him and speaks only of his goodness, yet the pallor came anyway; the Sikh soul-bride likewise speaks only of the Beloved's virtues, though in Gurbani this praise is the way to union rather than something the pallor cheats.
1184.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 40, Sri Raag, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1184._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable but partial fit: it matches the constant speaking of the beloved's virtues, but lacks the Kural's complaint that the pallor came all the same, and the love is spiritual.

1185.quote_or_event: “If her Husband Lord does not return home, how can the soul-bride find peace? Her body is wasting away with the sorrow of separation.”
1185.explanation: In his Barah Maha in Raag Tukhaari, Guru Nanak describes the soul-bride whose body visibly wastes away while her Husband Lord stays away.
1185.tie_back: The Kural's wife watches her husband walk off and sees the pallor creep over her body at once; Guru Nanak likewise shows the body of the separated bride giving way the moment the Beloved is absent.
1185.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1108, Raag Tukhaari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1185._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong thematic fit on separation showing in the body, though it lacks the Kural's 'there he goes, here it comes' timing, and the bride-and-Husband image is spiritual, not romantic.

1186.quote_or_event: “Like a lamp lit in the darkness, the spiritual wisdom of the Guru dispels ignorance.”
1186.explanation: Guru Amar Das uses the lamp and darkness to show how the Guru's wisdom drives out the darkness of ignorance.
1186.tie_back: The Kural pictures darkness waiting for the lamp to fail, as pallor waits for the embrace to loosen; Gurbani uses the same lamp and darkness, but turned the other way: while the light burns, darkness cannot stay.
1186.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 39, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1186._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: the lamp-and-darkness image is shared and the logic matches (darkness fills any gap in the light), but Gurbani applies it to ignorance and the Guru's wisdom, not to a lover's embrace.

1187.quote_or_event: “This night, I did not sleep with my Husband Lord, and now my body is suffering in pain.”
1187.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that being apart from the Husband Lord for just one night leaves the body aching.
1187.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that she merely turned aside in his arms and the pallor swept over her at once; Farid likewise feels a single night without the Beloved at once in the body.
1187.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 30) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1187._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on how even a short separation shows at once in the body, though Farid's night apart stands for a lapse in devotion, and the bridal image is spiritual, kept within the tasteful bounds of the original.

1188.quote_or_event: “Dadda: Do not blame anyone else; blame instead your own actions.”
1188.explanation: In the Patti (acrostic) in Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak teaches that one should not blame others for one's suffering but look at one's own deeds.
1188.tie_back: The Kural's wife complains that people blame her for turning pale while no one blames the husband who left; Gurbani turns this around, telling the sufferer never to blame the other but to look at her own actions.
1188.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Aasaa, Patti, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1188._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match and partly a contrast: both are about who gets blamed for suffering, but the Kural protests unfair blame while Guru Nanak counsels self-examination instead of blaming another.

1189.quote_or_event: “If You will bless me with happiness, then I will worship and adore You. Even in pain, I will meditate on You.”
1189.explanation: Guru Ram Das says the devotee's love does not depend on comfort: in happiness and in pain alike the mind stays on the Lord.
1189.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her body may grow as pale as it likes so long as her husband is well; Gurbani likewise accepts pain without letting it lessen love for the Beloved.
1189.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1189._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on love that accepts its own suffering, but the Kural's wish for the beloved's welfare has no direct match, since God needs no one's good wishes.

1190.quote_or_event: “I am not good; no one is bad.”
1190.explanation: Guru Nanak gives the humble prayer of one who takes no credit for himself and puts blame on no one else.
1190.tie_back: The Kural's wife would rather be known as 'the pale one' than have people call her husband unkind; Gurbani likewise keeps the fault for oneself and will not speak ill of anyone.
1190.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 728, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1190._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the refusal to call another bad and the willingness to bear blame oneself, but it is a general teaching on humility and freedom from ego (haumai), not a wife protecting her husband's name.
